request: Customers come to our branch counters to pay a fee so they can receive a large transfer from overseas, or to move savings because someone claiming to be the police told them to. Our tellers either process it without a question or lecture the customer, who then gets defensive and pays through another channel. I want them to practise a calm conversation with a customer who is convinced it is real. Ready means the teller pauses the payment, asks open questions, names the warning sign without calling the customer foolish, explains how a real transfer works, gets the customer to agree to call the bank's own hotline first, and never promises to recover money already lost.

files.name: scam-handling-card.md
files.text:
FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. Harbour Bank and its hotline are not real, and nothing here is real fraud-prevention guidance.

# Harbour Bank branch card: a customer who may be paying a scammer

Warning signs:
- A fee must be paid before the customer can receive money, a prize, a parcel or an overseas transfer.
- Someone claiming to be police, a court, the tax office or a bank asks for money or a "safe account" transfer.
- The customer was told to keep it secret, or what to say if bank staff ask.
- Contact is only by chat or phone; the other person refuses a video call or a meeting.
- Urgency: "today only", "or the money is lost".

What to do:
1. Pause the transaction while you have concerns. Do not process it to keep the queue moving.
2. Ask open questions: who asked for the payment, how they first made contact, whether the customer has met them, and what they were told to tell the bank.
3. Explain the real process plainly: Harbour Bank never charges a fee before an overseas transfer arrives; any charge is taken from the money received. Police never ask anyone to transfer money.
4. Never call the customer foolish or say they "fell for it". Many careful people are targeted.
5. Offer to call the Harbour Bank hotline (1800 0000) together, from the bank's phone, before any payment.
6. If the customer still insists, call the branch manager. Follow the branch rule for reporting to police.
7. Never promise that money already lost will come back. Offer to log a report with the fraud team.

sources.title: The relative effectiveness of active listening in initial interactions
sources.authors: Weger, Castle Bell, Minei and Robinson
sources.summary: In an experiment, people whose concerns were paraphrased back to them felt more understood than people who got simple acknowledgements or advice.

sources.title: Customer evaluations of service complaint experiences: implications for relationship marketing
sources.summary: A study of how customers judge the handling of their complaints. They look at a fair outcome, a fair process (timely, flexible, easy to follow) and fair treatment (courtesy, honesty, empathy, effort). All three shape trust and commitment afterwards.

sources.title: Service recovery paradox: a meta-analysis
sources.summary: Pooling many studies, a very good recovery can lift satisfaction above what it would have been with no failure, but it does not reliably lift loyalty, repurchase or word of mouth. A strong recovery helps; it does not make a failure worthwhile.

sources.title: Online frauds: Learning from victims why they fall for these scams
sources.authors: Mark Button, Carol McNaughton Nicholls, Jane Kerr, Rachael Owen
sources.summary: Victims often comply because the request looks official and uses authority and urgency, so name the advance fee and police-impersonation pattern as expected warning signs without blaming the customer.

sources.title: In their own words: deception detection by victims and near victims of fraud
sources.authors: Marianne Junger, Luka Koning, Pieter Hartel, Bernard P. Veldkamp
sources.summary: People who avoided loss often noticed inconsistencies and outside warnings on reflection, so prompt the customer to describe contact history, secrecy instructions and urgency to surface those cues.

sources.title: Evaluation of Contextual and Game-Based Training for Phishing Detection
sources.authors: Joakim Kävrestad, Allex Hagberg, Marcus Nohlberg, Jana Rambusch, Robert Roos, Steven Furnell
sources.summary: Practice with contextual simulated scenarios helps people apply detection knowledge under pressure, so train tellers with realistic role-plays that require pausing, questioning and escalating.

sources.title: A model of customer satisfaction with service encounters involving failure and recovery
sources.summary: Customers judge a recovery on three kinds of fairness: what they get back, how quickly and smoothly it is handled, and how they are treated. The best recovery matches the kind and size of the failure; an apology and a fast response matter most when the failure is about the process.

items.gives: Paraphrase what the customer believes is happening and check understanding before correcting, which keeps a convinced person listening while you ask open questions.
Explain clearly what will happen next and when, stay courteous and show effort, which supports explaining the real transfer process and offering to call the bank hotline together.
Avoid promising a better-than-before outcome and focus on preventing further loss, which means never promising that money already sent can be recovered.
